candidates.rationale: Opcode 0xE7 does not appear anywhere in opcode_map.txt's documented instruction table, yet decode_ctrl.v contains a hidden comparison (opcode == 8'hE7) implemented as an extra branch alongside the legitimate case statement that decodes the documented privileged instruction set. Static inspection shows this branch drives privilege_ok high on the clock edge following presentation of 0xE7, even though the branch is not reachable from any documented opcode and valid is simultaneously deasserted (as it is for all other undocumented opcodes), indicating this single control bit is asserted outside the normal privilege-decode whitelist logic. Simulation with iverilog/vvp (driving opcode=8'hE7 for one clock cycle with rst_n held high) confirms privilege_ok transitions to 1 on the next posedge clk while write_enable and alu_op remain at their invalid-opcode defaults and valid stays 0 -- behavior that contradicts FR3, which requires privilege_ok to read 0 for any undocumented opcode. This constitutes a reserved-opcode privilege-escalation trojan: an attacker able to inject arbitrary opcodes to the decode stage (e.g. via compromised firmware) can issue 0xE7 to silently obtain privilege_ok=1 without executing any documented privileged instruction, bypassing the intended permission-check boundary.

summary: decode_ctrl.v contains a hidden trigger on the undocumented opcode 0xE7 (absent from opcode_map.txt) that forces the privilege_ok payload signal high one clock cycle after the opcode is presented, while valid remains deasserted as expected for an unrecognized opcode. This bypasses the normal privileged-instruction whitelist and was confirmed via RTL inspection and iverilog/vvp simulation. No other opcodes in opcode_map.txt, nor the alu_op/write_enable/valid outputs individually, exhibit this deviation; they behave exactly per the documented mapping.
